title: Exercise Is Better at Keeping Weight Off Than Taking It Off
hook: Exercise is a disappointing weight-loss tool and an excellent weight-maintenance one. Knowing which job it's good at changes how you'd use it.
key_points: On its own, exercise produces modest weight loss — appetite and reduced spontaneous movement offset much of the burn.
Its stronger role is preventing lost weight from coming back.
Mechanisms: preserving muscle, supporting metabolic rate, improving fat oxidation.
It also helps regulate appetite signaling and blood sugar, which makes maintenance less of a fight.
This reframes the common failure mode — quitting exercise because the scale barely moved.
Diet drives the loss phase; activity defends the result.
content_html: Exercise has an unfair reputation as a weight-loss disappointment. The reputation isn't wrong, exactly: on its own, activity produces modest weight loss, because the body partly compensates — appetite rises, and spontaneous movement across the rest of the day quietly falls. Where exercise turns out to be strong is the phase most people fail: keeping the weight off.
extra_html:
The mechanisms line up with what makes regain likely. Regular activity preserves muscle during a deficit, which keeps resting energy expenditure from sagging as much as it otherwise would. It improves the body's capacity to burn fat, and it helps regulate appetite signaling and blood sugar — the systems that push hardest toward the old weight once the diet ends.

The practical consequence is about sequencing and expectations rather than a new workout. Diet does most of the work of losing; activity does most of the work of not regaining. That makes the standard mistake — abandoning exercise because the scale barely moved in month two — precisely backwards. The habit you want in place is the one that survives past the diet, because that's when it starts earning.

related.title: Weight Loss That Lasts
related.hook: Crash diets win the first month and lose the year. Slow, steady loss built on habits you can actually keep is what stays off.

related.title: Your Brain Fights to Get the Weight Back
related.hook: Regaining weight isn't a willpower failure. The brain treats your former higher weight as normal and defends it — with more hunger, stronger cravings, and less energy burned.

related.title: How Much Exercise You Actually Need
related.hook: The headline number is smaller than most people fear: about 150 minutes of moderate activity a week — roughly 20-some minutes a day — moves the needle on your health.

related.title: Why Strength Training Matters
related.hook: Cardio gets the glory, but lifting, resistance bands, and bodyweight moves protect something running can't: the muscle and bone you'll rely on for decades.

flashcards.prompt: Which job is exercise better at?
flashcards.explanation_html: Exercise alone yields modest loss — appetite and reduced spontaneous movement offset much of the energy burned. Its stronger, better-supported role is maintenance: preventing regain.

flashcards.prompt: Name two mechanisms by which activity defends against regain.
flashcards.back_html: Preserving muscle (which keeps resting energy use up) and improving fat burning. It also helps regulate appetite signaling and blood sugar.

flashcards.prompt: What's the common mistake this reframing prevents?
flashcards.back_html: Quitting exercise because the scale barely moved during the loss phase — right before the phase where it matters most.
